findings.body:
`dependencies = [("billing", "0007_add_reason")]` points at a migration this PR deletes. Django builds the graph from migration modules on disk, so `0008` is an orphan node: `manage.py migrate` cannot resolve `billing.0007_add_reason` and will fail before `RemoveField` runs.

**Failure mode:** fresh clones and CI that run migrations from this branch error immediately on graph load. Environments that already applied `0007` also lose the matching module while `django_migrations` still records it — `migrate` history checks break.

**Fix:** restore `migrations/0007_add_reason.py` and keep this `0008` as the forward drop. If `0007` was never applied anywhere, delete `0008` instead and only remove `0007`.

Deleting `0007_add_reason` removes the migration that introduced `invoice.void_reason`. Once any database has applied it, Django expects that module to remain forever so the graph and `django_migrations` rows stay consistent.

**Failure mode:** `migrate` / `showmigrations` on DBs that recorded `billing.0007_add_reason` raise inconsistencies; new environments never create the column then cannot run a dependent `RemoveField`. Schema history diverges across deploys.

**Fix:** put this file back. Ship a new `0008` with `RemoveField` only. Only delete `0007` (with no dependent `0008`) if you have proven zero environments ever applied it — and then do not add a drop migration that names it.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change breaks the Django migration graph and cannot apply cleanly in any environment that follows `billing.0007_add_reason`.

## What went wrong

`migrations/0008_drop_reason.py` declares `dependencies = [("billing", "0007_add_reason")]`, but the same commit **deletes** `migrations/0007_add_reason.py`. Django resolves the graph from files on disk; with the parent missing, `migrate` fails with a node/dependency error before any `RemoveField` runs.

## Correct approaches

- **Column already shipped / may exist in any DB:** keep `0007_add_reason` in the tree and add `0008` as a forward `RemoveField` (what 0008 already tries to do). Never delete an applied migration module.
- **`0007` never reached any database:** drop `0007` only and leave no `0008` that points at it. There is nothing to remove if the add never ran.

The PR combines both strategies and gets neither: it removes the add migration and adds a drop that still requires it.

## Data note

If `void_reason` exists and holds rows, `RemoveField` drops that data. The PR claims the field was never UI-surfaced; still confirm no writers/readers remain and that staging/prod either never applied `0007` or are ready for a deliberate column drop.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: `0008_drop_reason.py` depends on `billing.0007_add_reason`, but this PR deletes `migrations/0007_add_reason.py` and leaves no replacement on disk, so Django cannot resolve the migration graph. That matches the claimed failure for fresh clones/CI and applied environments.

`0007_add_reason.py` (AddField for `invoice.void_reason`) was deleted while `0008_drop_reason.py` still depends on `billing.0007_add_reason` and runs `RemoveField` on that column, so any DB that applied 0007 (or any fresh migrate through 0008) breaks the migration graph.
